items.title: Harbour Sports Club membership
items.context: A man phones a sports club to join.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Good morning, Harbour Sports Club, Emma speaking. How can I help?

transcript.speaker: Jonathan
transcript.text: Hi there. I'd like to become a member, please. I've just moved to the area.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Lovely. I can take your details over the phone and get the form started for you. Could I have your name first?

transcript.speaker: Jonathan
transcript.text: Yes, it's Jonathan Fairfax.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Could you spell your surname for me?

transcript.speaker: Jonathan
transcript.text: Of course. It's F-A-I-R-F-A-X.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Fairfax, thank you. And what's your address?

transcript.speaker: Jonathan
transcript.text: It's 72 Weston Road. Oh, sorry, no, that was my old flat. It's number 27 Weston Road.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: 27 Weston Road. And the postcode?

transcript.speaker: Jonathan
transcript.text: It's BH6 4TR. That's B-H-6, then 4-T-R.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Great. What's the best phone number to reach you on?

transcript.speaker: Jonathan
transcript.text: There's a landline at the house, but I'm hardly ever in. My mobile is best. It's 07734 519208.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: 07734 519208. Thanks. Now, we like to know which activities members are most interested in, so we can send the right timetables.

transcript.speaker: Jonathan
transcript.text: Well, I was thinking about tennis, but I hear the courts are booked up most evenings. So I'd say swimming, mainly in the evenings after work.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Evening swimming. The pool's open until ten, so that should suit you.

transcript.speaker: Jonathan
transcript.text: Perfect.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: And which type of membership would you like? We have individual, couple and family.

transcript.speaker: Jonathan
transcript.text: I was going to go for individual, but my wife and our two kids want to come along too, so I think family makes more sense.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: No problem. And would you prefer to pay annually or monthly?

transcript.speaker: Jonathan
transcript.text: Monthly, please. How much would that be?

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: The individual rate is 38 pounds a month, but the family membership is 45 pounds a month, and that covers two adults and up to three children.

transcript.speaker: Jonathan
transcript.text: That's very reasonable.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Can I ask how you heard about us? Was it through our website?

transcript.speaker: Jonathan
transcript.text: No, actually. A neighbour mentioned you, but what made me call was a poster I saw in the library.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Oh good, so they did put it up. Now, when would you like your membership to start?

transcript.speaker: Jonathan
transcript.text: Could I start on Monday?

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: I'm afraid the pool is closed on Mondays this month for maintenance. How about Tuesday?

transcript.speaker: Jonathan
transcript.text: Tuesday's fine.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: And one last thing. When you come in, please don't use the south car park, because it's being resurfaced. Use the north car park, which is right next to the main entrance.

transcript.speaker: Jonathan
transcript.text: The north car park. Got it. Thanks so much for your help.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: You're welcome, Mr Fairfax. We'll see you on Tuesday.

items.title: Ashford Maritime Museum
items.context: A guide welcomes a group of visitors to a maritime museum.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Ashford Maritime Museum. My name's Daniel, and I'm one of the volunteer guides here.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Before you head off to explore, I'd like to give you a quick introduction to the building and tell you what you'll find in each area.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: A lot of visitors assume this building was once a fish market, because the fish quay is just outside the front door.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: In fact, it was built in 1842 as the town's customs house, where merchants paid tax on the goods their ships brought in.
keywords: built in 1842 as the town's customs house

answerTags.after: built in 1842 as the town's customs house

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: It only became a museum in the 1970s, after the shipbuilders' warehouse next door was knocked down.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Now, some news for regular visitors. Entry is still seven pounds for adults, I'm afraid, so it hasn't become free, although under-sixteens still get in without paying.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: What has changed is that since April we've extended our opening hours, so we now close at six rather than five.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: We're also hoping to launch an audio guide app, but that won't be ready until next year.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: So, where to start? Most people go straight into the Harbour Gallery, but I'd suggest you begin with the short film in the Orientation Room.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: It's only twelve minutes long and it gives you a timeline that makes everything else much easier to follow.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: A quick practical point: reception no longer has space to store luggage, so any large bags must go in the lockers on the lower ground floor.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Right, the areas themselves. The Harbour Gallery has our collection of oil paintings of the port.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Some of them are very fragile, so please keep your cameras and phones away in there. Photography isn't allowed in that gallery at all.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Next door is the Shipwreck Room. We used to run free guided talks in there, but these days it's self-guided.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: The highlight is the original captain's log from the Mary Ellen, along with letters written by her crew, the real documents, not copies.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Then there's the Lighthouse Tower. You can climb all ninety steps, but it costs an extra two pounds on top of your ticket.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: People expect a spectacular view from the top, but to be honest the windows are rather small.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: On the first floor you'll find the Rope Workshop. At eleven and at two, one of our volunteers shows you how rope was made by hand, so you can watch the whole process live.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: If you have children with you, head for the Children's Deck. They can dress up as sailors, try tying knots and steer a model ship, so it's all hands-on.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: I should mention that the Navigation Room on the same floor is temporarily closed while we repair the roof.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: And finally, the Captain's Café on the top floor. The cakes are excellent, but the real reason to go up is the terrace.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: From there you get the best view of the town and the whole harbour, much better than from the tower.
keywords: the best view of the town

answerTags.after: the best view of the town

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: The café stays open until half past five, so there's plenty of time.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: If you have any questions, you'll find me or one of the other guides in the entrance hall.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Enjoy your visit, everyone.

items.title: Choosing a research topic
items.context: A tutor and a student, Maya, discuss her research project.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: Come in, Maya. Have a seat. How's the project planning going?

transcript.speaker: Maya
transcript.text: Better, I think. I've narrowed it down to two ideas since our last meeting.
keywords: narrowed it down to two ideas

answerTags.after: narrowed it down to two ideas

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: Good. I know you were worried about the proposal deadline, but that's not for another fortnight, so there's no rush.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: So, you mentioned last week you were thinking about urban noise.

transcript.speaker: Maya
transcript.text: I was, and there's actually plenty of research on it. But honestly the data collection would have taken the whole term. I'd need readings from dozens of sites.
keywords: data collection would have taken the whole term

answerTags.after: data collection would have taken the whole term

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: That's a fair point. So what have you settled on instead?

transcript.speaker: Maya
transcript.text: I did consider air quality in city parks, but I'm leaning towards rooftop gardens and how they affect building temperature.
keywords: rooftop gardens and how they affect building temperature

answerTags.after: rooftop gardens and how they affect building temperature

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: Interesting. There's quite a lot published on that already, isn't there?

transcript.speaker: Maya
transcript.text: There is, which is actually why I like it. It won't save me any time reading, but I can compare my results with earlier studies.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: Good. And where would you take your measurements? Not in the lab, I hope.

transcript.speaker: Maya
transcript.text: No. The library has a green roof, and the facilities team said I could use it from next month.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: Make sure you get that permission in writing. Facilities staff change, and you don't want to lose access halfway through.

transcript.speaker: Maya
transcript.text: I'll email them today. What about equipment? I'd looked at buying temperature loggers online, but they're quite expensive.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: Don't spend your own money on them.

transcript.speaker: Maya
transcript.text: No, I'll borrow temperature loggers from the geography department instead. They have about twenty.
keywords: borrow temperature loggers from the geography department

answerTags.after: borrow temperature loggers from the geography department

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: Twenty should be plenty. Now, the timetable. Your literature review was originally due in week four, but we've moved it. It needs to be finished by week six.

transcript.speaker: Maya
transcript.text: Week six. OK. Should I include studies from other countries?

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: Yes, and they don't all have to be recent ones. But focus on cities with a similar climate to ours, otherwise the comparison won't hold.

transcript.speaker: Maya
transcript.text: That makes sense. I'd also thought about interviewing the building managers.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: That would be nice to have, but it's not essential. I'd leave it unless you have spare time.

transcript.speaker: Maya
transcript.text: Fair enough. And the final report, is it still four thousand words?

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: Three and a half thousand, plus appendices. And keep the method section short. Examiners care much more about your analysis.

transcript.speaker: Maya
transcript.text: Got it. Short method, more analysis.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: Is there anything else you're unsure about?

transcript.speaker: Maya
transcript.text: Not right now. I'll send you a draft outline by Friday.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: Perfect. Good luck, Maya.

items.title: Urban heat islands
items.context: A lecturer explains why cities are warmer than the countryside and what can be done about it.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Good afternoon. Today we're looking at a phenomenon that affects almost every large city on the planet: the urban heat island.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Put simply, an urban heat island is a built-up area that is noticeably warmer than the countryside around it.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The effect was first described in the early nineteenth century by Luke Howard, an amateur scientist who is better known for naming the clouds.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Howard kept careful temperature records in London and compared them with readings taken in nearby villages.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: So how big is the difference? You will sometimes read that city centres can be twelve degrees warmer, but that figure comes from a single, very unusual night.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: A more typical maximum is around seven degrees, and in most cities the average difference is much smaller.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Interestingly, the gap is not greatest in the middle of a hot afternoon, as you might expect.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: It is actually at night that the difference is most marked, because the city releases the heat it has stored during the day.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: That brings us to the causes. The first is the materials we build with.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Dark surfaces, and asphalt in particular, absorb a great deal of solar energy and then give it off slowly for hours.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Concrete and brick behave in a similar way, though they are generally a little paler.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The second cause is the lack of vegetation. In the countryside, plants and moist soil cool the air through evaporation.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: In a city, rainwater is quickly carried away by drains, so there is far less moisture available for this natural cooling.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The third cause is waste heat. Vehicles contribute, of course, but a surprisingly large share is released by buildings, through heating systems, lighting and machinery.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: And the shape of the city matters too: tall buildings along narrow streets trap warm air and block the wind.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Why does any of this matter? Hotter cities use more energy for cooling, and air pollution tends to be worse.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: But the most serious concern is health. During heatwaves, the group most at risk is the elderly, particularly those who live alone.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Young children are also vulnerable, but studies consistently show the highest death rates among older people.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: So what can planners do? One simple approach is so-called cool roofs.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: These are roofs painted white or covered with light materials so that they reflect sunlight rather than absorbing it.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Another is to increase green space. Many people assume that grass is enough, but in fact it provides relatively little cooling.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The most effective measure is planting trees along streets, because they provide shade as well as releasing moisture.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Finally, cities need better data. Here in our own city, researchers originally planned to use weather balloons.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Instead, they attached two hundred small sensors to lampposts, which now record temperature every ten minutes.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The results have already shown which neighbourhoods need the most urgent attention.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: In next week's session we'll look at some of that data in detail, so please read chapter five before then.
